title: Ontario nurses at a breaking point share stories of stress and burnout in a new report
summary: A new report shares first-hand testimonies from Ontario nurses who describe enduring burnout, anxiety and distress working in understaffed and under-resourced hospitals in the province. The report's…

image.caption: A nurse attends to a COVID-19 patient in the Humber River Hospital intensive care unit in January 2022. A new report that shares the testimonies of nurses working in Ontario hospitals is meant to shed light on the realities facing the profession. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: As an Ontario nurse dealt with a chaotic shift, her mind raced between priorities: "Am I going to make the palliative patient comfortable? Am I going to try to save the drug user? Or am I going to get the naked and confused woman off the floor? What am I going to do?"
These are the concerns shared by a medical-surgical nurse named Jane — a pseudonym used to protect her identity — in a new report on the state of nursing care in Ontario.

She painted a scene of urgency and confusion as she attempted to split her attention among five high-need patients. Jane said she asked for help, but everyone else was overwhelmed with their own patients.

During the shift, she said, her patient in palliative care died, leaving her with thoughts of frustration and fear, like, "Am I actually going to be conscious of someone’s last breath, or will I be sued because I had to leave a patient unattended in the washroom?"

The report, co-authored by James Brophy and Margaret Keith, adjunct professors in the department of sociology at the University of Windsor, was released on Monday by the Ontario Council of Hospital Unions (OCHU), the hospital division of the Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE). It's a collection of interviews and testimonies from 14 Ontario hospital nurses who describe the realities of working in hospitals they say are understaffed and under-resourced.

blocks.text: One nurse using the pseudonym Sumaia described not having working equipment and computers to do her job. Another, called Kim, said she'd seen an increase in violence against health-care staff and witnessed another nurse knocked unconscious by an ER patient.

Brophy says the nurses are describing a level of burnout and moral injury — mental distress caused by the inability to provide patients with necessary care — that's become the new norm. He says the issue is reaching a tipping point.
Attention on retention: what's causing nurses to leave?
"We're talking nurses that have been practising 15, 20, sometimes 30 years, who simply cannot tolerate it any longer," Brophy said. "They're looking to leave the profession."

In a recent Nanos Research survey of 551 nurses in Ontario, roughly eight in 10, said they're fearful one of their patients might be harmed because they have so many demands and are unable to provide timely care.

Of the nurses surveyed, 88 per cent said they experienced exhaustion as a result of work, 73 per cent said they felt anxiety and roughly half said they are considering leaving their jobs within the next year because of working conditions.
Other studies suggest these sentiments are shared by nurses across the country, especially among young nurses.
According to a report by the Montreal Economic Institute, for every 100 nurses under the age of 35 who registered to practise nursing in Canada, 34 did not renew their registration in 2024.

items: N.L. has Canada's worst retention rate for young nurses, report finds

blocks.text: The problem is particularly acute in Newfoundland and Labrador, which saw 61 nurses under the age of 35 leaving for every 100 entering.
According to a 2018 study cited by the Canadian Federation of Nursing, the country is projected to be short 117,600 nurses by 2030.

Brophy says while the unbearable strain nurses are under is well documented in surveys, their first-hand experiences typically go unheard because health-care workers often don't speak publicly for fear of retribution.
"Their voices are muted," said Brophy.

James Brophy, adjunct professors in the department of sociology at the University of Windsor, is the co-author of a report titled We are in Survival Mode about the state of nursing in Ontario. (Jonathan Pinto/CBC)
"The approach in a qualitative study like this is to put flesh on the bones," he said. "We're trying to show what the real-life experience is."
He says a common concern nurses have is their inability to offer a good quality of care to patients beyond just administering clinical care.

For example, he says nurses working with adequate staffing and support are afforded the ability to detect and report domestic violence. Nurses say they can also be a source of crucial comfort to patients processing difficult diagnoses or end-of-life transitions.
He says the public's attention needs to be turned to these nurses who are sounding the alarm. "I really hope that … the average person is outraged by what they're reading."
The health of health-care workers

Kelsey Toney of Milton, Ont., told CBC News that becoming an emergency nurse had been a dream of hers, but after six years working as a registered nurse in the Peel area, from working in hospitals largely because of inadequate staffing.
"I felt like I was being asked to care for too many patients at once," she said. "I wasn't willing to have my licence put in jeopardy."
Toney says during her time working in hospitals, she experienced "close calls" that threatened her safety and became burnt out, especially while working during the pandemic.
"I think my career in health care was partly putting my own health at risk."

items: It's my dream to become a nurse, but the unpaid work nearly broke me

blocks.text: Now self-employed working in medical esthetics, Toney says she's seen a significant improvement in her work-life balance.
Toney says she doesn't see herself returning to work in a hospital due to low wages and the way the current health-care system is set up.
"I don't have the support that I need to make sure that the patients are getting adequate care."
Safer nurse to patient ratio

Angela Hodgson, a registered practical nurse (RPN) in Kingston, Ont., and chair of the RPN Committee of OCHU-CUPE, says nurses in Ontario hospitals are breaking inside and want to see the implementation of minimum nurse-to-patient ratios.
Already implemented in some jurisdictions, mandatory minimum nurse to patient ratios of 1:5 in medical and surgical units were found to reduce occupational injury and illness rates in California.

Nurses from across British Columbia rally for better working conditions and other requests in downtown Vancouver in February 2025. In 2024, B.C. became the first province in Canada to implement a mandatory minimum of one nurse for every four patients in medical and surgical units. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

British Columbia became the first province in Canada to implement a mandatory minimum of one nurse for every four patients in medical and surgical units. And Manitoba passed legislation in June to enact minimum nurse to patient ratios, though it has not yet been implemented.

Hodgson says a safer number of nurses per patient would allow care providers to better understand and prioritize patient needs, alleviating strain on nurses and also improving quality of care for patients.
"When you have four patients, it's doable. But when you have six patients, seven patients, eight patients, there's so many duties that are required of that nurse to complete," she said.
"Everybody says, ‘nurses are angels and they're heroes,' and they put you on this pedestal, but we are humans and we can only handle so much."

blocks.text: Valerie Grdisa, CEO of the Canadian Nurses Association says stories of moral distress and burnout are present among nurses across the country and the Canadian health-care system needs to be redesigned.

She says while there's no easy fix for nursing burnout in Canada, some changes that need to be made include investing more in primary and home care, preventative health measures and increased staffing.
"We are proud of our health system," she said. "But we could do way better."
